## 4 · Margin normalisation opportunity (what closing the gap is worth)

For every product **below** the portfolio margin, `Uplift` = revenue × (portfolio margin − product margin): the gross profit available at current volume if the product traded at the portfolio average margin. This is an *accounting* re-valuation, not a demand forecast — it is the prize to stress-test with the pricing simulator (elasticity may claw part of it back).

| Product | Category | Revenue | Margin | Uplift at portfolio margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lego Bricks | Toys | $2,388,883 | 12.5% | $365,166 |
| Rubik's Cube | Games | $912,983 | 10.0% | $162,367 |
| Magic Sand | Art & Crafts | $968,962 | 12.5% | $148,071 |
| Splash Balls | Sports & Outdoors | $541,630 | 11.1% | $90,266 |
| Dino Egg | Toys | $420,214 | 9.1% | $78,538 |
| Toy Robot | Electronics | $305,357 | 19.2% | $26,111 |
| Animal Figures | Toys | $507,766 | 23.1% | $23,837 |
| PlayDoh Playset | Art & Crafts | $157,387 | 16.0% | $18,545 |

**Total opportunity across all below-par products: $981,971** at constant volume (before any elasticity effect).

## 8 · Elasticity stance (what we do and do not claim)

- Historical prices are **static** (1 price per product, verified in the data-quality gate: `max price levels per product = 1`).
- Therefore demand elasticity **cannot be estimated** from historical price variation. Any elasticity figure would be fabricated. We do not do that.
- The Excel simulator and Power BI report use a **Scenario-Based Pricing Simulation**: price change and elasticity are analyst inputs, and the volume response `ΔQ = E_d × ΔP` is labelled as an explicit assumption (baseline `E_d = −1.2`).
